options: One single value
A list of values
A whole table
Any of these, Postgres picks one
why: One value goes after `>` or `=`. A list goes after IN. A table goes in FROM.

q: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)` returns no rows at all, and some manager_id values are NULL. What happened?
options: Postgres ignored the NULL, so the answer is correct
NOT IN with a NULL in the list is never true, so every row is rejected
The subquery ran too slowly and timed out
NOT IN only works with numbers
why: Never use NOT IN on a list that can hold a NULL. Use NOT EXISTS.

options: A subquery that is saved and shared between queries
A subquery that always returns exactly one row
A subquery that uses a column of the outer row, so it runs once for each outer row
A subquery inside a WITH
why: Without an index on what it looks up, running once per outer row can be slow.

q: You write a JOIN and then add DISTINCT to remove copies, only because you want stores that have at least one order. What fits better?
options: UNION
A second DISTINCT
GROUP BY on every column
EXISTS
why: If you add DISTINCT after a JOIN to remove copies, you probably wanted EXISTS. It answers yes or no and makes no copies.

q: What does `WITH recent AS (SELECT ...)` give you?
options: A named step that the later parts of the query can read like a table
A table saved on disk for other queries
A faster index on the result
A lock on the rows inside it
why: A CTE is a list of named steps. It lives only for that one query.
